James Glendinning
jāmz glen-din'-ing
n. (James Glendinning, fl. 1622–1630, minister at Oldstone in county Antrim, the unlikely instrument of the Six Mile Water revival)
Hebrew Ya'aqob, Jacob, a heel-catcher, supplanter; Glendinning, a Dumfriesshire place-name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

James Glendinning was a graduate of Edinburgh and a native of Scotland who came over to Ulster about 1622 and was placed first at Carrickfergus, where Robert Blair judged him unfit for a town charge and advised his removal to a country parish. At Oldstone, near Antrim, he became the first instrument of the Six Mile Water revival. He had, by every account that survives, one note only. He preached the law, the wrath of God and the terrors of judgment with such force that hearers fell down in the church and went home unable to eat or sleep; and he had nothing whatever to say to a wounded conscience afterward. The neighbouring ministers were sent for to do the work he could not do, and the awakening that followed was in a real sense built upon a ministry that God used and then set aside. Glendinning himself ended badly. He fell into visions and date-setting, went off toward Rome to convert the pope, and was last heard of wandering in Asia Minor. His case is a standing warning and a standing comfort: the power is not in the vessel. “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jer 23:29).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines terror as extreme fear, and zeal as passionate ardour in the pursuit of any thing.

Modern Corruption

A one-note preacher of terrors whom God used and then laid aside.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Glendinning does, however, stand against two errors at once. He rebukes the modern pulpit that will not name wrath, for God plainly honoured the naming of it; and he rebukes the man who concludes from his usefulness that he was sound, for he was not. Scripture declines to flatter zeal on its own: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2).

The principle to recover is that law without gospel wounds without healing, and that this is a defect in the minister and not in the method of God. The letter kills and the Spirit gives life (2Co 3:6); Oldstone needed Antrim and Bangor and Templepatrick before its broken men were bound up.

Usage

"“like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces” (Jer 23:29) — Oldstone under his preaching."

"“a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — the man himself."

"“the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life” (2Co 3:6) — why others had to be sent for."
